author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: After three centuries, the legendary 'lost' Williamson's World — colonized by the first human to leave the Solar System — is finally rediscovered.
page_summary:
After three centuries, the legendary 'lost' Williamson's World — colonized by the first human to leave the Solar System — is finally rediscovered. Relay official Edward Rogers arrives expecting a triumphant reunion, but finds a deliberately archaic, decentralized society of self-sufficient farm 'manors,' complete with ritual clan warfare, that has received the Galaxy's technological broadcasts for a century and simply chosen not to use them. Rogers explains that the uniform, centrally-coordinated Galactic Relay culture exists specifically to prevent war between divergent societies, and presents Articles of Incorporation for Williamson's World to formally join. The planet's leader and his people, after a private vote, refuse. Rogers reluctantly delivers an ultimatum — join within six hours or be destroyed — and when the planet's antiquated jet-rocket fleet rises in a doomed, symbolic defense, the Galactic battleship annihilates the entire world without difficulty. The story closes far from these events, on Corporal Pete Matson returning home on leave to give his young son a 'souvenir' — a handmade wooden cup, taken, unknowingly to the boy, from the world just destroyed to prevent exactly the kind of cultural variation that produced it.

**Why it matters.** The story's argument is structural rather than stated: Rogers's own justification for destroying Williamson's World — that uniform culture prevents war — is undercut by the fact that achieving and maintaining that uniformity itself requires an act of overwhelming, one-sided violence against anyone who declines to participate. The story never allows Rogers to be simply wrong or simply right; his genuine regret, and the Relay's genuinely stated peaceful rationale, sit uncomfortably alongside the fact that an entire distinct human culture, populated by people with names, customs, and a coherent way of life, is annihilated without survivors. The closing shift to Corporal Matson's family — utterly separate from and ignorant of the preceding events — refuses the reader any character within the story who understands the full moral weight of what has happened, leaving that recognition entirely to the reader alone.

*The boy's wondering repetition of the unfamiliar word 'souvenir,' and the 'strange light' that 'grew' in his eyes as he turns the cup from the destroyed world in his hands, closes the story on an image of innocent wonder built directly on an atrocity neither he nor his father will ever understand.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: discovery and cultural encounter, ultimatum and refusal, and a final ironic domestic coda
movements: Rogers arrives at the newly rediscovered Williamson's World and learns its people have deliberately rejected Galactic technological and cultural uniformity in favor of an archaic, clan-based agrarian society.
Rogers presents Articles of Incorporation; the planet votes to refuse integration, and Rogers is forced to deliver an ultimatum of destruction within six hours.

The planet's token, doomed resistance is annihilated instantly; the story closes on a soldier from the destroying fleet bringing home an innocent souvenir from the now-erased world for his unknowing family.
structure.point_of_view: third person, close to Rogers for the bulk of the story, then shifting in its final scene to Corporal Matson's family, so the reader alone carries the full, devastating context that the story's own characters (Matson's wife and son) never learn.
structure.central_device: A closing scene of ordinary domestic warmth (a father's homecoming gift) deliberately staged to be read, by the reader alone, as the final harvest of an entire planet's annihilation — dramatic irony used to indict the callousness of the preceding genocide rather than to soften it.

characters.name: Edward Rogers
characters.note: Genuinely moved by Williamson's World and reluctant to see it destroyed, yet never once considers refusing his orders or advocating for an alternative — his personal regret coexists entirely comfortably with his execution of policy.

characters.name: Gene Williamson
characters.role: leader of the colony, descendant of its founder
characters.note: Calmly, clearly articulate about his people's deliberate choice to reject Galactic uniformity, his people's culture rendered with enough specificity and dignity that their destruction reads as tragedy rather than as the elimination of mere primitives.

characters.name: Corporal Pete Matson
characters.role: a soldier in the destroying fleet, unrelated to the story's main action until its final scene
characters.note: His genuine tenderness toward his wife and son, and total ignorance of what his 'souvenir' actually represents, makes the story's closing irony land as an indictment of ordinary complicity rather than of any single villain.

settings.name: Williamson's World
settings.note: Rendered with careful specificity — clan wars, communal manors, artisanal crafts, a common if fading language — establishing a genuine, coherent alternative culture rather than mere backwardness, which is precisely what makes Relay's justification for its destruction so troubling.

settings.name: The Matson household, elsewhere
settings.note: An entirely ordinary domestic scene, deliberately disconnected in tone and knowledge from the preceding genocide, its warmth curdled retroactively by what the reader alone understands the 'souvenir' to be.

motifs: A centrally enforced cultural uniformity justified as the only guarantee against war, itself enforced through the threat and execution of total destruction
A doomed, symbolically futile defense (antiquated rockets against a modern battleship) undertaken anyway, in preference to cultural erasure
Dramatic irony deployed in a story's closing scene to indict complicity rather than to comfort the reader
An innocent object (a souvenir) carrying, unknown to its recipients, the full weight of an atrocity

distinctive_terms.label: Rome
distinctive_terms.note: Williamson's manor-based clan culture is explicitly compared to Roman and medieval antecedents, giving it historical depth rather than mere invented strangeness.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No commentary by Dick on this specific story was found. The evidence gatherer's one hit (a joking reference to a 'silk pillow with Souvenir of Fullerton stitched on it' in a personal letter) and the one criticism hit (a bibliography citation of 'Souvenir Press,' a UK publisher) are both excluded here as false positives on the word 'souvenir' rather than genuine commentary on this story.

open_questions: Is there documented commentary from Dick on this story's use of dramatic irony in its closing scene, given how sharply it differs in tone from the preceding action?
Is Rogers's uncomplicated compliance with an order he personally regrets ever discussed by critics as an early example of Dick's recurring interest in bureaucratic complicity in atrocity?
Is there secondary criticism comparing this story's central conflict (enforced cultural uniformity vs. deliberate cultural divergence) to Dick's later, more developed treatments of the same tension?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
